To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the effects of fungicide treatments on the recovery of seeds from the seed bank differed between wetlands and upland meadows, 2) seeds of exotic species were recovered at higher rates than seeds of native species in upland meadows but not in wetlands, 3) the effects of fungal pathogens on seed recovery did not differ between native and exotic species in either habitat.

(1) fungal seed pathogens may contribute to species exclusion from wetlands, (2) fungal seed pathogens did not contribute to the success of exotic species over natives, and (3) seed pathogens offer poor prospects for biocontrol of most exotic plants. 4.1.
fungal pathogens may play a role in limiting the distribution of native species, but that they have little influence on the distribution and success of invasive species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of pathogens and herbivores on seedling establishment and survival.
the influence of pathogens in the soil seed bank on the survival of buried seeds of a broad range of native and exotic plant taxa.
the effects of soil fungi on the seed banks of a taxonomally broad suite of congenerics, native and exotic plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fungal pathogens have a limited effect on the invasion of plants.
the hypothesis that low seed pathogen load is one of the factors that contribute to the success of exotic species is not true.
fungal seed pathogens do not play a significant role in the invasion success of exotic plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fungal pathogens may have a greater influence on the invasion success of native vs. exotic plants, but that the effects of fungal pathogens on native vs. exotic seeds are similar.
fungal pathogens are not a major factor in the invasiveness or success of exotic species.
fungi are not the primary reason why exotic plants are more successful than natives.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of seed pathogens as biocontrol agents for invasive species is not likely to be an effective management tool.

the effects of seed pathogens may not be a useful criterion for distinguishing between exotic species that are invasive and native species that are not, and thus are unlikely to be a useful criterion to use for the management of invasive species.
seed pathogens are not a good target for the biocontrol of exotic plants.
